title: Conjecture 1.3 (Small conjecture)
statement_text: A class of graphs closed under induced subgraphs is small if and only if it has bounded twin-width.
context_text: Small classes contain at most $n! \cdot c^n$ graphs on vertex set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ for some constant $c$. This conjecture generalises the Stanley-Wilf conjecture to graphs, motivated by Theorem 1.2 which establishes one direction: classes with bounded twin-width are small. The conjecture was proposed in a previous paper in the twin-width series.
paper_contribution: Disproves the conjecture by constructing (via Theorem 1.1, a finitely generated group with infinite twin-width) a small class of graphs closed under induced subgraphs with unbounded twin-width (Corollary 1.4).
notes: Conjecture header reads '(Small conjecture [3])'; reference [3] is a previous paper in the twin-width series. PDF extraction — bibliography not fully visible.

title: Informal Conjecture (uniform twin-width strictly stronger than twin-width)
statement_text: Uniform twin-width is strictly stronger than twin-width, i.e. there are groups with finite twin-width and infinite uniform twin-width.
context_text: Twin-width is a graph (and ordered 0–1 matrix) parameter: a graph has twin-width at most $k$ if it can be reduced to a single vertex by successively merging two vertices, marking as red the edges to vertices adjacent to only one of the two merged parts, so that every intermediate graph has red degree at most $k$; for an ordered 0–1 matrix, rows and columns are merged only between consecutive ones. A finitely generated group has finite twin-width if some (equivalently every) Cayley graph has finite twin-width (this is invariant under quasi-isometry for bounded-degree graphs); equivalently, there is a total order $<$ on $\Gamma$ such that for every $x\in\Gamma$ the permutation matrix of the right-multiplication action of $x$ on $(\Gamma,<)$ has finite twin-width (for permutations, finite width in the sense of Guillemot and Marx, i.e. avoiding some pattern), which also defines finite twin-width for non-finitely generated groups. The uniform twin-width of $\Gamma$ is the minimum over total orders $<$ of $\sup_{g\in\Gamma}$ of the twin-width of the action of $g$ on $(\Gamma,<)$, i.e. it requires a bound on these twin-widths that is uniform over all $g$, so finite uniform twin-width implies finite twin-width. Finite uniform twin-width is preserved by group extensions (hence direct and semidirect products), infinite direct products and sums, direct limits, finite-index supergroups, quotients by finite subgroups and wreath products, and the authors show that abelian, solvable and polynomial-growth groups, lamplighter groups and automorphism groups of trees have finite uniform twin-width. The converse implication is not established. A proposed candidate separating the two notions is the group of finitely supported permutations of $\mathbb{Z}$: it has finite twin-width, but finite uniform twin-width for it would imply a universal bound on the uniform twin-width of finite groups and, more generally, of elementary amenable groups, which the authors find unlikely.
notes: Stated in prose in Section 1.2 with 'We conjecture that'.

title: Question (explicit group with infinite twin-width)
statement_text: Can we find a more explicit construction of a group with infinite twin-width, or one with a direct proof that twin-width is infinite?
context_text: Twin-width is a graph (and ordered 0–1 matrix) parameter: a graph has twin-width at most $k$ if it can be reduced to a single vertex by successively merging two vertices, marking as red the edges to vertices adjacent to only one of the two merged parts, so that every intermediate graph has red degree at most $k$; for an ordered 0–1 matrix, rows and columns are merged only between consecutive ones. A finitely generated group has finite twin-width if some (equivalently every) Cayley graph has finite twin-width (this is invariant under quasi-isometry for bounded-degree graphs); equivalently, there is a total order $<$ on $\Gamma$ such that for every $x\in\Gamma$ the permutation matrix of the right-multiplication action of $x$ on $(\Gamma,<)$ has finite twin-width (for permutations, finite width in the sense of Guillemot and Marx, i.e. avoiding some pattern), which also defines finite twin-width for non-finitely generated groups. The authors construct a finitely generated group with infinite twin-width, using Osajda's theorem on embedding graphs into groups; this disproves the 'small conjecture' (that every small hereditary graph class, i.e. with at most $n!\,c^n$ labelled graphs on $n$ vertices, has bounded twin-width). The construction starts from a sequence of bounded-degree graphs with unbounded twin-width (which exist by counting: almost all $3$-regular graphs have large twin-width) and relies largely on probabilistic methods. No explicit or deterministic construction of bounded-degree graphs with unbounded twin-width is known; since the subgraphs of a Cayley graph of a group with infinite twin-width form a bounded-degree class of unbounded twin-width, a more explicit group, or one with a direct proof of infinite twin-width, could solve that problem and significantly help understanding twin-width.
notes: Stated as a question in prose at the end of Section 1.3.

title: Open Problem (separating twin-width and queue number on sparse graphs)
statement_text: Separating twin-width and queue number on sparse graphs is an open problem.
context_text: The queue number of a graph is the least $t$ such that, for some vertex order, the edges can be partitioned into $t$ sets none containing two nested edges $xy,uv$ with $x<u<v<y$. Twin-width is a graph (and ordered 0–1 matrix) parameter: a graph has twin-width at most $k$ if it can be reduced to a single vertex by successively merging two vertices, marking as red the edges to vertices adjacent to only one of the two merged parts, so that every intermediate graph has red degree at most $k$; for an ordered 0–1 matrix, rows and columns are merged only between consecutive ones. A finitely generated group has finite twin-width if some (equivalently every) Cayley graph has finite twin-width (this is invariant under quasi-isometry for bounded-degree graphs); equivalently, there is a total order $<$ on $\Gamma$ such that for every $x\in\Gamma$ the permutation matrix of the right-multiplication action of $x$ on $(\Gamma,<)$ has finite twin-width (for permutations, finite width in the sense of Guillemot and Marx, i.e. avoiding some pattern), which also defines finite twin-width for non-finitely generated groups. Bounded tree-width implies bounded queue number, which implies bounded twin-width. Queue number is also a group invariant (via Cayley graphs), and is characterised by excluding decreasing sequences in the adjacency matrix for some vertex ordering, which allows a uniform queue number for groups to be defined in analogy with uniform twin-width; many results of the paper also hold for queue number. Yet the authors know no group with finite twin-width and infinite queue number (nor for the uniform variants), and they state that separating bounded twin-width and bounded queue number on sparse graphs (e.g. bounded-degree graphs) is an open problem.
notes: Explicitly declared an open problem in Section 1.4.
